sections.html: Eigenmannia males grow considerably larger than females. The largest Eigenmannia reported to date was about 50 cm long; however, many apparently remain under 20 cm. The animals in the photos are currently 9-12 cm long.

Glass knifefishes (Eigenmannia) are widespread throughout the South American subcontinent. E. virescens, described in 1836, is found in the Rio la Plata and lower Paraná in Brazil, Argentina, Uruguay and Paraguay, but it is questionable whether this southern species has been imported more frequently. The fish described here come from Venezuela and are referred to in recent scientific papers as E. sp. “Orinoco”.
Their favorite food is red mosquito larvae, but they will also eat other, comparable food, usually also granules.
These animals establish a hierarchy among themselves, but are generally considered peaceful.
Males grow considerably larger than females. The probable male of the photographed pair is yellow and the probable female is gray-white.
The glass knifefish observed so far have spawned in the roots of floating plants.

The genus is difficult and very complex systematically; today 32 species are known. The “Orinoco” form shares the pattern of three black longitudinal stripes with E. trilineata, but has an undershot mouth (lower jaw significantly shorter than the upper jaw), whereas in the “true” E. trilineata the mouth is terminal. From an aquarium point of view the species affiliation is rather irrelevant, as all Eigenmannia are similar in behavior, so they are usually referred to as E. virescens.
